drills.q: Name the three Core Web Vitals with their good thresholds and what each measures, and state which lab tool score is NOT the same thing as passing them.
drills.a: LCP<2.5s (loading), INP<200ms (responsiveness, replaced FID March 2024), CLS<0.1 (visual stability), graded at p75 over CrUX's rolling 28-day window of real users. A high Lighthouse score is a synthetic lab number on a fixed simulated profile and is not equivalent to passing CWV in the field.

drills.q: A page's LCP is 4.2 seconds. Walk through how you'd diagnose which of the four LCP phases is the bottleneck.
drills.a: Use web-vitals attribution data (or DevTools Performance panel) to separately measure TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time, and element render delay. The fix depends on which dominates: slow TTFB -> server/CDN; large load delay -> resource not discoverable early (client-rendered); large load time -> resource size/compression; large render delay -> render-blocking CSS/JS ahead of the element.

drills.q: Why is blanket-applying loading="lazy" to every image on a page a mistake, with real numbers?
drills.a: Applying it to the actual LCP image delays its discovery/download. Measured field data: p75 LCP moves from 364ms to 720ms and the share of good pages drops from 79% to 52%. Lazy-load should apply only below-the-fold images; the LCP candidate should get fetchpriority="high" instead.

drills.q: What is a long task, and why can a click handler that itself runs in only 10ms still produce bad INP?
drills.a: A long task is main-thread JS execution over 50ms without yielding, blocking input processing and paint. INP includes processing time AND presentation delay, not just handler execution -- a fast handler that triggers an expensive synchronous downstream re-render, or one queued behind an already-running unrelated long task, still produces bad INP.

drills.q: Give the prioritized remediation order for a slow, INP-hurting click handler, and explain why a Web Worker isn't always the first move.
drills.a: Order: (1) chunk work and yield between chunks (scheduler.yield/setTimeout fallback) (2) move heavy CPU-bound compute to a Web Worker (3) defer non-critical work via requestIdleCallback (4) reduce DOM work via virtualization. A Web Worker adds serialization overhead and no DOM access -- worth it for genuinely CPU-heavy self-contained work, but if the cost is mostly triggering a large synchronous render, yielding or reducing render scope is cheaper and more targeted.

drills.q: Name the three most common real causes of CLS and the fix for each, then explain why CLS can look fine in local dev but spike for slow-connection users.
drills.a: 1) Unreserved image/embed dimensions -> width/height or aspect-ratio. 2) Font swap metric mismatch -> font-display:optional or size-adjust matching. 3) Content injected above existing content -> reserve space or overlay. On fast connections the font/resource often arrives before first paint, masking the shift; on slow connections there's more time between paint and arrival, making the swap/shift visible -- test CLS under throttled network conditions.

drills.q: A React SPA ships a 2.3MB initial bundle. Give a prioritized reduction plan with realistic expected impact, and state when more code splitting stops helping.
drills.a: First, route-based code splitting (React.lazy/dynamic import) -- commonly gets initial critical-path bundle to ~100-150KB with rest loaded per route. Second, tree shaking plus swapping heavy deps (moment.js -> date-fns). Combined, 60-80% total reduction is realistic. Third, add a CI bundle-size budget to prevent regression. More splitting stops helping when it increases network round trips on high-latency connections or forces multiple sequential fetch-then-execute chunks synchronously on interaction, hurting INP.

drills.q: Your team ships a performance fix; Lighthouse CI shows clear improvement but CrUX field data shows no change three weeks later. What's going on, and how would you get faster feedback?
drills.a: CrUX uses a rolling 28-day window, so a fix needs real traffic to accumulate before the number moves -- three weeks may not be enough data yet. Separately, Lighthouse's fixed simulated profile may not represent your real traffic mix. Get faster feedback by instrumenting your own RUM (web-vitals library reporting to your own analytics backend) rather than waiting on Google's delayed, aggregated CrUX report.

drills.q: Explain font-display: swap vs font-display: optional, when to choose each, and what size-adjust does mechanically.
drills.a: swap shows fallback text immediately and swaps in the custom font whenever it loads (good for LCP, risks CLS on swap). optional gives ~100ms grace; if missed, the fallback is used for the entire page view with zero swap and zero CLS risk, at the cost of sometimes never showing the custom font. Choose optional when zero CLS matters more than brand-font guarantee; choose swap + size-adjust when the font must eventually appear. size-adjust is a font-face descriptor that scales the font's metrics to match a fallback, computed from the numeric difference between the two, minimizing the reflow when swap does occur.

drills.q: Two pages have identical Lighthouse scores but very different real-world INP. Explain why, how you'd find the actual difference, and why the fix for a 'growing list' culprit is virtualization rather than per-item render optimization.
drills.a: Lighthouse runs a short interaction script on a simulated profile and doesn't capture real session length or accumulated state (memory growth, a list grown large through use) that degrades field INP. Find the difference via RUM attribution data (which interaction, which element) rather than blind lab reproduction. Virtualization is the durable fix because at sufficient list length even a well-optimized per-item render still means O(n) DOM nodes and reconciliation work scaling with data size -- virtualization changes the complexity class rather than shaving a constant factor.
